strengths: The paper identifies a useful distinction between explaining predictions through raw inputs and through interpretable macro-level features. Its discussion of hidden confounding caused by omitted concepts is relevant to researchers in explainability and algorithm auditing.

Using PAGs and FCI provides an established framework for representing latent confounding and partial causal identification. The restriction that predictions cannot cause image content supplies sensible background knowledge without requiring access to model internals.

The synthetic example clearly illustrates the intended distinction between a possible causal feature and a feature associated through hidden confounding. The two applications, bootstrap analyses, and alternative discovery algorithm demonstrate a concrete workflow.

The exposition is generally accessible and thoughtfully discusses explanatory goals, background assumptions, annotation errors, and limitations of automatically constructed features. This methodological application has an identifiable audience without needing a new discovery algorithm.
weaknesses: Necessary: Correct the interpretation of the reported feature rankings. Section 6.3 combines directed and circle-arrow edges, although a circle-arrow edge remains compatible with purely confounded association. Moreover, absence of adjacency to the prediction does not exclude an indirect causal effect: Figure 10 contains Cardiomegaly circle-arrow Atelectasis → prediction, despite Cardiomegaly receiving zero adjacency stability. Report definite and possible ancestry separately, distinguish stability from evidence of causal importance, and revise the causal-irrelevance statements in Sections 6.3–6.4 and the figure captions.

Necessary: Address selection in the X-ray experiment. The 240 images comprise 120 pneumonia cases and 120 controls selected specifically for having no findings. Inclusion therefore depends on diagnosis and the explanatory findings, potentially inducing selection associations. This conflicts with the dismissal of selection bias in Section 3 and undermines the subsequent causal edge interpretations. Analyze the selection mechanism, use an appropriate sampling design, or explicitly withdraw the unsupported causal conclusions from this application.

Necessary: Establish the reliability of the conditional-independence tests or narrow the empirical conclusions. With 26 multilevel bird attributes and conditioning sets up to size four, contingency tables can be very sparse even with 3,538 images; the X-ray analysis has only 240 images and potentially rare findings. Expected-count diagnostics and handling of sparse tables are not reported, and bootstrapping does not repair test miscalibration. The acknowledged sensitivity is substantial: Crown Color moves from zero FCI stability in Figure 8 to the highest GRaSP-FCI stability in Figure 15. These results leave the specific bird-feature conclusions unresolved.

Necessary: Clarify and repair the causal interpretation of the Shapley counterexample in Section 3.3 and Appendix A. The omitted-feature calculation retains the unobserved z3 as a fixed input; it is not the observational adjustment estimator using only Z2. Meanwhile, several 'valid' coalition expectations leave Z1's distribution unchanged when intervening on its parents Z2 or Z3, so they are not generally the SCM's intervention expectations. Define the coalition game and estimand precisely and compare valid and invalid identification of that same quantity, or replace the example. The current calculation does not convincingly isolate hidden-confounding bias.

Optional: An association-based explanation using the same semantic annotations would help distinguish the benefit of causal discovery from the benefit of changing explanatory units. Intervention checks on generated images and clearer reporting of which data split supplies the discovery samples would also strengthen validation and reproducibility.
